marisol.title: Margin Notes
marisol.text:
Past closing, Marisol drags two tall stools into the cramped back office and takes three ledgers down from the top shelf. They're bound in leather, and each has her father's crest stamped on the cover, rubbed nearly smooth.

She opens the first one under the lamp. His figures run down the middle of every page in a big, confident hand. Hers are in the margins. There are years of them, in red ink, small and furious and exact. She corrected his tallies to the half-copper. She traced one debt through three false buyers. In one corner a twelve-year-old has written THIS IS WRONG and underlined it twice.

"I used to leave these open on his desk," she says. Her gold hoops sway as she turns the page. "He'd close them without reading and tell me I had a good head."

She taps a column with an inky thumb and doesn't look up.

"He never listened to me once. You actually do, Sam. I haven't decided what to do about that."
ngpp: Flipping backward through red columns, she freezes suddenly staring at an old ink flourish—like she's already shown you this exact dusty ledger page once before.
"Wait—why did I set the red inkwell beside your left elbow instead of your right, Sam?" Marisol mutters sideways, eyeing her own hand sharply.
She slides the margin open straight toward your nose without hesitation. "No idea why my pulse speeds up whenever you lean over these accounts, Sam—just read the red ink."

choices.label: Ask her to walk you through one
choices.res: Marisol props her leather-bound travel ledger squarely between you on the desk and runs a sharp fingernail down six-year-old spice tariffs, maritime interest tables, and stubborn debts crossed out twice in faded red ink. You listen carefully through every single sum without glancing once toward the clock—and at the end she shuts the heavy clasp gently, as though someone had finally finished reading her story aloud.

choices.label: Tell her the margins are the best part
choices.res: "The margins are honestly the best part," you tell her straight, tapping a dry satirical tally scribbled underneath an old captain's penalty. Marisol stares blankly across the oak desk for three heartbeats, clearly unprepared for someone actually reading her private jokes—then grabs a quill, slashes a hurried secret line beside Tuesday's salt prices, grins sharp as cut brass, and locks the book.

image.comp: showing him old ledgers covered in her margin notes, leaning over a desk together
image.setting: owner's office, stacks of ledgers, lamplight

marisol.title: Invoice Ambush
marisol.text:
You're in the tub with your eyes shut when the washroom door bangs open.

"The linen invoice is wrong again, and before you say anything, I have the last three months right here." Marisol is waving a fistful of paper. She gets four steps into the room before she sees where you are.

She doesn't stop. She has never once given ground in the middle of an argument, and it seems she isn't going to start now.

"Twelve sheets billed, nine delivered. Second point." Her gold hoops swing with every item. Her eyes have gone up to the ceiling, and they stay there, as though the rest of her case were written on it. "Second point, the laundress is his cousin."

She's on her third point now. You're too wet to take notes. A drop of condensation falls from the ceiling onto the invoice, and she keeps going.

1.title: Settling Balances
1.text:
Marisol kicks the washroom door open with an invoice in her hand, as usual. Then she sees you waist-deep in the steam, and she shuts the door quietly behind her and drops the latch.

The invoice goes onto the dry shelf. She sits down on the bath bench and leans over the rim, close enough that her hoops swing forward and her curls start to frizz in the heat.

"You still owe me two silver for Tuesday's wine, Sam." Her eyes move down your chest to the waterline and come back up without any hurry. "I've been thinking about how to collect. Are you paying in coin, or in labor?"

choices.label: Pull her down to the tub edge and pay up properly
choices.res: Her competitive smirk cracks instantly into a breathless laugh as you tug her flush against the cedar rim, wet palms gliding smoothly under her skirt until the invoices are forgotten completely.
choices.fallbackRes: She grins crookedly and hooks two fingers under your wet chin, kissing you warm and slow through the steam before drying off her cuffs.

choices.label: Splash warm water on her blouse and call it settled
choices.res: She squeaks as hot spray hits her collar, then dumps a whole wooden scoop back over your head laughing wildly.

image.comp: sitting on the bath bench leaning over the rim, hoops swinging, curls frizzing in the heat, eyes moving down slowly, teasing look

3.title: Waterproof Ledger
3.text:
Marisol doesn't bring any paper into the washroom tonight.

She stands beside the steaming tub and unbuttons her blouse, looking at you the whole time. Her dark curls are already sticking to her collarbones. The blouse goes over the stool, and the skirt follows it, and then she steps over the rim naked and sits down in the hot water facing you, with her knees against yours.

"New house policy, Sam." She leans forward until her tits brush your chest. "Any dispute after nine gets settled in the tub, with nothing on. I have several disputes."

choices.label: Pull her onto your lap in the hot water
choices.res: You catch her waist neatly without checking a single sum and pull her bare body straight across your lap into the hot, sloshing cedar bathwater—gold hoops swinging brightly past your jaw as Marisol locks her thighs smoothly around your hips and kisses you fierce and breathless to settle the argument her way.

choices.label: Keep the water slow and tease her breathless
choices.res: You hold her slick waist comfortably against the warm cedar rim and begin teasing her patiently through the drifting steam—slow hands tracing every curve along her ribs, collarbones, and thighs while Marisol tilts her chin defiantly until her crisp breath breaks into hot, unguarded gasps.

image.comp: stepping into the hot water naked and sitting facing him, knees against his, leaning forward with breasts brushing his chest, curls on collarbones, sly smile

choices.label: Argue back from the tub
choices.res: You keep your voice impeccably crisp over the steam and walk her point-by-point through two supplier credits she somehow double-billed on Wednesday afternoon. Against every rule of her proud life, Marisol runs out of math first—yet snaps her fingers sharply toward your soaking collar to inform you wet men carry zero procedural standing before stalking out to slam the door with her chin held impossibly high.

choices.label: Ask for some privacy
choices.res: She flashes an exasperated eye-roll that makes her heavy gold hoops ring like altar bells, slaps the damp invoice squarely down beside the spare sponge, and stalks cleanly over the threshold to yank the washroom door shut with commendable volume. Two heartbeats later her knuckles rap twice sharply on the painted wood from the hall: "Have that settled cleanly by Friday afternoon, Takahashi."

choices.label: Splash her
choices.res: Open naval warfare breaks out cleanly inside two seconds flat. Steam turns to flying bathwater as your palm sends a wave straight over the cedar lip, soaking her neatly pressed wool cuffs from wrist to hem. Marisol screeches in pure delighted outrage, snatches the heavy soaking sponge from the bench, and hurls it straight at your chest while half the landing eavesdrops laughing.

image.comp: standing in a washroom doorway waving an invoice, mid-argument, not leaving
image.setting: steamy wooden washroom, a man in the tub off-frame

marisol.title: House Rules
marisol.text:
Marisol challenges you to cards in the lounge on a slow night, and you learn that she grew up playing against dockhands.

She beats you four times in a row. She snaps each winning hand down on the table with relish, and her curls bounce. She keeps the score on the back of a receipt in red ink, and she adds it up aloud.

The fifth hand, you win. You can't work out how. She had two queens and she folded to a bluff so bad that you'd been embarrassed to make it.

You look at your cards, and you look at her.

"I wanted to see your face," she says.

Then she laughs until she can't breathe. She has one hand pressed to her ribs and her hoops are swinging, and there are tears in her eyes. You've never seen her laugh like that. You think she probably didn't do much of it in this room, growing up.

choices.label: Demand a rematch, with stakes
choices.res: With a single wide sweep of your forearm you scatter the marked cards cleanly over the floorboards and clear the inkwell straight off the oak ledger desk. Marisol shrieks with pure, bright triumph, kicking off her heeled boots on the spot as you catch her by the waist and haul her bare thighs straight up onto the warm wood to settle the wager immediately.

choices.label: Demand a week's ledger stakes
choices.res: You slap down the whole week of dusty back-office tallies on the table without flinching and lose cleanly two rounds later to her wicked third pair of queens. Marisol taps her chin darkly, circling your chair slowly while letting you name your own humiliating forfeit—and takes a remarkably long, breathless time finding an objection when your voice drops low near her collarbone.

choices.label: Admit that your face was worth it
choices.res: "Honestly worth every last silver coin just for that look," you laugh, tossing your bent hand straight into the discard stack across the oilcloth. Marisol freezes mid-shuffle, blinks hard to clear the sting in her eyes—and for once in a long life of sharp merchant ledgers fails completely to produce a cutting comeback, silently dealing out one fresh unhurried round just for the two of you.

image.comp: slapping a winning hand of cards on the table, laughing at his face
image.setting: staff room at night, cards and coins on the table

marisol.title: A Letter
marisol.text:
A letter comes for Marisol on the morning boat. It's creased and stained with salt, and the hand on the front is one she has been looking for in the post for a long time.

Her father is alive. He's across the sea, in a port town with a warm climate. He writes that he's well and that he misses her cooking. In the last paragraph he mentions that he's in some difficulty over money, and that it's nothing she should worry about.

She reads it three times at the ledger desk with her jaw set.

Then she starts going through the house accounts, looking for something to sell. She tries the good glassware, and then her mother's earrings. The ink on her fingers has started to smear the letter.

"He doesn't even ask," she says. "He just leaves it lying there where I'll trip over it. He knows exactly what I'm like." Her voice cracks on the last word.
ngpp: Staring down at the sea-stained postmark, Marisol frowns uneasily—as if some stubborn instinct already warns her how clean a refusal feels.
"Funny, Sam—I swear we sat at this desk until sunrise crossing out that old fool's numbers once before," she mutters softly without looking up.
She lays the salt-stained letter calmly under your thumb without raising her voice. "Skip the argument, partner. Help me tell him no cleanly, like we do."

choices.label: "No. He left you with all of this."
choices.res: "He is NOT your father!" Marisol snaps with enough fury to rattle the ink bottles on your shelf, yanking the oak door open so hard her bright gold earrings chime like warning bells down the stairs. She keeps clear of your corridor for half an evening—before knocking quietly next noon with two hot honey cakes and an equally quiet apology that earns yours cleanly back.

choices.label: Send him 300g
choices.res: She stands frozen beside the tall desk window, staring silently at the crisp stack of silver you push across the ink-stained blotter without raising your voice. Ten slow seconds crawl by before Marisol lets out a sharp, unsteady breath. "You didn't have to pay off a single copper of his mess," she murmurs roughly. "I know," you answer simply, and watch her shoulders finally drop.

cantAfford.res: You can't spare it. She understands. Mostly.

choices.label: Help her write back
choices.res: It takes three pots of cooling spiced tea, four torn sheets in the grate, and half the quiet hours until blue light hits the window glass—yet together you draft a brisk, polite, airtight note closing the family credit cleanly without leaving cruelty on paper. When the wax finally cools across the seal, she drops her head calmly onto her folded sleeve beside your inkwell and sleeps straight through.

image.comp: reading a letter with a stricken expression, his hand on her shoulder

marisol.title: Her Mother
marisol.text:
Before the noon rush, Marisol asks if you have an hour. She doesn't say what for.

She walks you up the steep goat path behind the east ward, to the top of the hill where the wind comes in off the sea. There's a small pale headstone in the meadow grass, and one faded silk ribbon is tied around it.

It's her mother's.

For the first time since you met her, Marisol isn't moving. The gold hoops hang still. Both her hands are deep in her coat pockets. She watches the gulls turn over the harbor below.

"She kept the books before I did," she says after a while. "She taught me the red ink. He didn't start making mistakes until she was gone." She breathes out. "I come up here when I've balanced a hard month, to tell her. I've never brought anyone with me. I wanted her to see who I'm working with."

2.text:
Before the noon rush, Marisol walks you up the goat path behind the east ward to the small pale headstone in the meadow grass. The sea wind is cold today. She reties the faded ribbon without speaking and stands back.

Then she puts her hand straight into the pocket of your hoodie, beside yours, and laces her fingers through them. She leans her whole weight against your shoulder.

"I told her about you last month," she says. "I said you could count, and that you listen. I didn't tell her the rest." Her thumb moves across your knuckles. "I think she's worked it out. She always knew what I wanted before I did."

image.comp: standing close at a small headstone, hand tucked in his pocket laced with his, leaning her weight against his shoulder, quiet tender look

choices.label: Bring flowers
choices.res: She gathers the fresh hill blooms carefully beside the pale granite edge and spends the whole slow descent down the goat path telling you three small stories about her mother she has never spoken aloud to any soul in Hollowmere—burnt lemon loaf on market days, off-key harbor lullabies, and sharp household sums scribbled hastily in flour across the backs of old wine invoices.

choices.label: Just stand with her
choices.res: You don't try filling the wind-swept hilltop with clumsy comfort or borrowed speeches; you simply stand close enough for your coat sleeve to shelter her shoulder and lace your warm fingers firmly inside hers. After three quiet minutes Marisol leans her whole crisp, proud weight sideways against your ribs, watching pale afternoon cloud shadows cross the stone meadow beside you.

choices.label: Lead her quietly back into your parlor once you return
choices.res: Back inside your quiet house away from the brisk harbor wind, neither of you bothers lighting the hallway sconces before pulling your private office bolt cleanly shut. Marisol slips slowly out of her heavy wool coat without checking a single waiting sheet on the table, burying her warm cheek straight against your collarbone before tilting her chin deliberately up toward your mouth.

image.comp: standing at a small grave on a hill with him, holding wildflowers, quiet
image.setting: hilltop graveyard above a fantasy town, overcast

marisol.title: A New Deed
marisol.text:
Marisol asks you to come to the ledger room after closing, and to bring the deed.

The candle is guttering on the desk where she did her sums as a child. She takes the deed from you and reads it through once. Then she tears it in half.

Before you can speak, she has pulled a fresh sheet toward her and started to write. Her ink-stained fingers are perfectly steady. She copies the terms out in full, from memory, and at the bottom she writes two names where there used to be one.

"Partners," she says, and turns it around for you to sign. "In the house, and in the debt, and in the rest of it. In every sense, Sam. Don't make me say it twice. I can do sums all night, but I'm no good at this part."

Then she comes around the desk and kisses you. Her hoops are cool against your cheek. She reaches past you and shuts the door, firmly.
ngpp: Right as she tears the old deed, her hands pause for half a beat—smiling sideways as though this ink already belongs beside your name.
"Wait—did I already write two names on this exact parchment line in some fever dream, Sam?" she laughs breathlessly, pulling you closer.
"Every ledger in Hollowmere can burn to ash and reset at dawn, partner," Marisol whispers fiercely against your lips. "My name only ever sits beside yours."
marisol.goLead: Marisol tosses the quill aside and sweeps the ledgers off the edge of the desk with her forearm. She pulls you hard against her by the waist in the candlelight.

choices.label: Not yet
choices.res: Marisol slides the fresh ink-wet house deed neatly back across the desk and taps the single blank witness line right beside her own flourishing signature with the feather tip of her quill. "I can wait," she tells you smoothly, bright dark eyes holding yours without blinking once. "Only don't let the ledger cool too long—my ink stays ready when you are."
